items.title: Hatshepsut: Was This Really Egypt's Greatest Pharaoh?
items.content:
What does it take to be a great ruler? Rameses II, Akhenaten, Seti I- the great Egyptian Pharaohs- would have you believe it's building towering monoliths and waging great wars. But shouldn't it be someone who maintains peace, manages diplomacy to create a flourishing and healthy civilisation?

This is something the Pharaoh Hatshepsut was extraordinarily good at. In the 18th dynasty, she oversaw one of the most prosperous times in Ancient Egyptian history, expanded its influence further and made its people richer than ever before. Joining Dan to argue her case is Dr Campbell Price, curator of Egypt and Sudan at Manchester Museum.

Produced by Mariana Des Forges and edited by Natasha Hughes and Dougal Patmore.

items.title: The Early Life of William Shakespeare
items.content:
Long before he was The Bard, William Shakespeare was a broke, teenage father hustling to survive London’s cutthroat theatrical underworld. Navigating the deadly bubonic plague, family debt and brutal rivalries, how did an ordinary tradesman's son become a world-famous master playwright?

Dan Snow is joined by Rory Loughnane, author of 'Shakespeare at Thirty', to look at the luck, talent and gritty hustle that forged The Bard.

Produced by James Hickmann and edited by Dougal Patmore.

items.title: How Rasputin Destroyed the Romanovs with Anthony Beevor
items.content:
How did a Siberian mystic catalyse the downfall of the 300-year-old Russian Empire?

In an era defined by brutal industrialisation and the butchery of World War I, Russia's isolated autocracy was collapsing from the inside out. Bound to the royal family by the agonising secret of Tsarevich Alexei’s illness, the mysterious monk Grigori Rasputin became the court's ultimate pariah and the people’s chief villain.

Dan Snow is joined by renowned historian Sir Antony Beevor, author of 'Rasputin: And the Downfall of the Romanovs', to investigate Rasputin and the scandalous twilight of the House of Romanov.

Produced by James Hickmann and edited by Matthew Wilson and Dougal Patmore.

items.title: A Deep Dive on Submarines
items.content:
For centuries, humans have been fascinated by the mysteries of the deep sea. The history of submarines is one of extraordinary invention, daring exploration and deadly warfare. From the first experimental underwater vessels of the 17th century to the devastating U-boats of the First and Second World Wars, submarines have transformed naval warfare and revolutionised our understanding of the oceans.

Today, Dan visits the Royal Navy Submarine Museum in Gosport and is joined by curator Alexandra Geary to discover the eccentric origins of underwater travel and the dramatic submarine battles of WWI and WWII in honour of the 125th anniversary of the Royal Navy Submarine Service. He also speaks to Vice Admiral Sir Tim McClement, who was Second in Command on HMS Conqueror during the sinking of the Argentine ARA General Belgrano warship in the Falklands, as well as First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins on how AI might shape the submarines of the future.

With huge thanks to Commander James 'Dally' Dalrymple and Annarose Hearsum.

Produced by Mariana Des Forges, Beth Donaldson and edited by Dougal Patmore

items.title: WWI's Stalingrad: The Siege of Przemyśl
items.content:
Bread cut with sawdust. Horses boiled to the bone. Men trading pet dogs and mice for scraps.

In the brutal winter of 1914 to 1915, the grand Austro-Hungarian fortress of Przemyśl came under siege. Cut off by Russian armies and doomed by the vanity of their own generals, the garrison survived by the skin of their teeth until a final, desperate breakout charge…

Dan Snow is joined by Alexander Watson, author of ‘The Fortress’, to step inside WWI’s longest, bloodiest siege.

Produced by Mariana Des Forges and James Hickmann, edited by Natasha Hughes and Dougal Patmore.

items.title: The Rise of Peter The Great
items.content:
In 1698, a 6’8” Russian giant went on a bender through an English gentleman’s estate. He trashed portraits, burned furniture and drunkenly rammed wheelbarrows through a prize-winning holly hedge. The giant in question was Peter the Great, and this wasn’t just a royal lads' holiday; it was - ostensibly - statecraft.

In this episode, Dan Snow is joined by historian Daniel Beer to unpack the life of Russia’s most ruthless moderniser - from dodging Kremlin bloodbaths to building a brand new capital atop a mountain of human bones.

Produced by James Hickmann and edited by Dougal Patmore.

items.title: Medieval Ghost Stories
items.content:
Ghost stories have haunted conversations since ancient times, from the Mesopotamians to the Romans to the Vikings. The medieval period was particularly awash with ghost stories - after all, it was an era of great plague, piety and corporal punishment. Ghost stories served as useful tools to uphold hierarchies and manipulate the masses - live in accordance with the bible or be visited by a restless spirit... or become one yourself. To delve into some of the most popular ghost stories of medieval Britain and what the restless dead can tell us about the anxieties of the living, Dan is joined by Dr Eleanor Janega, historian and host of the Gone Medieval podcast.

Produced by Mariana Des Forges and edited by Natasha Hughes.

items.title: Charles de Gaulle: The Man Who Rebuilt France
items.content:
In June 1940, France was collapsing. Paris was in enemy hands, the government had fled, and Marshal Pétain was preparing to surrender. Into that chaos stepped a lanky, rigid French general with no army, no government and almost no followers - Charles de Gaulle. From penniless exile to twice head of state, his career would span two world wars, the collapse of empire, and the birth of modern France.

Dan Snow is joined by Richard Vinen, author of 'The Last Titans: Churchill and de Gaulle', to unpack the extraordinary, contradictory life of this formidable statesman.

Produced by James Hickmann and Dougal Patmore. and edited by Tim Arstall.
